cards.back: To leave hurriedly and secretly, typically to escape detection or arrest. Example: 'The accountant absconded with millions before the audit could be completed.'
Sharp and forthright in tone, especially of a comment or style of speaking. Example: 'The critic's acerbic review of the novel sparked a heated debate among literary scholars.'
To increase the power, status, or wealth of someone or something, often excessively. Example: 'The biographer accused the politician of using public office to aggrandize herself.'
Brisk and cheerful readiness to do something. Example: 'The graduate student accepted the research fellowship with alacrity.'
A deep-seated feeling of dislike or aversion. Example: 'The philosopher's antipathy toward reductionism shaped much of her later work.'
Approval or praise, especially of a formal or official nature. Example: 'The dissertation earned the approbation of every member of the review committee.'
Characterized by severe self-discipline and abstention from all forms of indulgence. Example: 'The monks led an ascetic lifestyle devoted entirely to contemplation and study.'
To make an unpleasant feeling less intense; to relieve or ease. Example: 'The dean attempted to assuage faculty concerns about the proposed curriculum changes.'
Having or showing an extreme greed for wealth or material gain. Example: 'The novel portrays the industrialist as an avaricious figure willing to exploit workers for profit.'
Demonstrating aggression and willingness to fight. Example: 'The nation's bellicose rhetoric alarmed neighboring countries and international observers.'
The making of false and defamatory statements about someone to damage their reputation. Example: 'The scientist endured years of calumny before her groundbreaking theory was finally accepted.'
To cease to resist an opponent or demand; to surrender. Example: 'After months of negotiation, the faculty union capitulated to the administration's revised contract terms.'
Given to sudden and unaccountable changes of mood or behavior. Example: 'The capricious funding decisions of the agency made long-term research planning nearly impossible.'
Clear, logical, and convincing in argument or reasoning. Example: 'The defense attorney presented a cogent argument that cast doubt on the prosecution's key evidence.'
Feeling or expressing remorse for having done wrong. Example: 'The researcher issued a contrite apology after acknowledging errors in the published data.'
Behavior in keeping with good taste and propriety; dignified conduct. Example: 'The moderator reminded panelists to maintain decorum during the academic debate.'
Causing harm or damage, especially in a subtle or unexpected way. Example: 'Prolonged exposure to the chemical had deleterious effects on the subjects' respiratory systems.'
To remove moisture from something, causing it to dry out completely. Example: 'The arid climate desiccated the soil, making agriculture unsustainable without irrigation.'
Intended to teach, particularly in having moral instruction as an ulterior motive. Example: 'Critics found the novel overly didactic, arguing that its moral lessons overshadowed the storytelling.'
Modest or shy because of a lack of self-confidence. Example: 'The diffident researcher hesitated to present her findings at the international conference.'
To conceal one's true motives, feelings, or beliefs. Example: 'The witness attempted to dissemble, but the cross-examination revealed inconsistencies in her testimony.'
To cause someone to feel drained of energy or vitality. Example: 'The grueling pace of the doctoral program enervated even the most dedicated students.'
Lasting for a very short time; transitory. Example: 'The ephemeral nature of social media trends makes them a challenging subject for longitudinal study.'
To use ambiguous language so as to conceal the truth or avoid committing to a position. Example: 'The politician equivocated when asked directly about her stance on the proposed tax reform.'
Having or showing great knowledge or learning. Example: 'The erudite professor effortlessly connected themes from ancient philosophy to modern neuroscience.'
To criticize someone or something severely. Example: 'The editorial excoriated the administration for its handling of the public health crisis.'
Very attentive to and concerned about accuracy and detail. Example: 'The archivist's fastidious cataloging preserved centuries of correspondence for future scholars.'
Producing or capable of producing an abundance of offspring or new growth; intellectually productive. Example: 'The fecund imagination of the novelist produced over thirty works in a single decade.'
Excessively talkative, especially on trivial matters. Example: 'The garrulous lecturer frequently digressed from the syllabus, much to the students' frustration.'
Devoid of guile; innocent and without deception. Example: 'The diplomat's guileless manner disarmed even the most suspicious negotiators.'
A lengthy and aggressive speech directed at someone. Example: 'The department chair delivered a harangue about declining standards at the faculty meeting.'
A person who attacks or criticizes cherished beliefs or institutions. Example: 'The philosopher was regarded as an iconoclast for challenging the foundational assumptions of her discipline.'
Unchanging over time or unable to be changed. Example: 'The laws of thermodynamics are considered immutable principles of the physical world.'
Just begun and so not fully formed or developed; rudimentary. Example: 'The student's inchoate thesis lacked the structure and evidence needed for a convincing argument.'
Lacking flavor, vigor, or interest; dull and uninspiring. Example: 'The reviewer dismissed the essay as insipid, noting its failure to engage with any original ideas.'
Using very few words to express oneself; concise to the point of seeming rude. Example: 'The professor's laconic feedback on the paper consisted of a single word: insufficient.'
Very generous or forgiving, especially toward a rival or someone less powerful. Example: 'In a magnanimous gesture, the winning team publicly praised the research contributions of their competitors.'
Not telling the truth; lying habitually. Example: 'The investigation revealed that the executive had been mendacious in her testimony to the regulatory board.'
Stubbornly refusing to change one's opinion or course of action. Example: 'The obdurate committee rejected all proposed amendments despite overwhelming faculty support.'
Obedient or attentive to an excessive or servile degree. Example: 'The obsequious assistant agreed with every suggestion the director made, regardless of its merit.'
Not able to be seen through; difficult to understand or explain. Example: 'The theorist's opaque prose made the article virtually inaccessible to readers outside the field.'
Excessively concerned with minor details or rules, especially in teaching. Example: 'The pedantic grader deducted points for every missing comma in the bibliography.'
Carried out with a minimum of effort or reflection; mechanical. Example: 'The committee's perfunctory review of the proposal overlooked several critical methodological flaws.'
Holding firmly to an opinion or course of action despite difficulty or opposition. Example: 'The pertinacious researcher continued her fieldwork for a decade until she finally proved her hypothesis.'
Having an unemotional and stolidly calm disposition. Example: 'The phlegmatic chairman remained unfazed even when the debate turned contentious.'
Spending money or resources freely and recklessly; wastefully extravagant. Example: 'The university's prodigal spending on administrative expansion drew criticism from faculty and students alike.'
Having an obstinately uncooperative attitude toward authority or discipline. Example: 'The recalcitrant student refused to revise the paper despite repeated feedback from the instructor.'
Optimistic or positive, especially in a difficult situation. Example: 'Despite the failed experiment, the principal investigator remained sanguine about the project's long-term prospects.'
Reserved or uncommunicative in speech; saying little. Example: 'The taciturn scholar published prolifically but rarely spoke at academic conferences.'
Bitter and abusive in language or criticism. Example: 'The vituperative exchange between the two economists dominated the pages of the academic journal for months.'
